item.title: LLM Fine-Tuning Workloads: Characterization, Challenges, and Opportunities for Serverless AI
item.description: arXiv:2610.40983v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Serverless execution of Large Language Models (LLMs) is becoming important, reflecting their wide societal use. An increasingly present stage in LLM pipelines is fine-tuning, which specializes trained models and improves inference performance. Serverless operation of LLM fine-tuning workloads shifts operational concerns from the user to the provider. For these new workloads, providers face important operational complexities, such as performance issues, resource waste, and even service failure due to misconfiguration. However, optimizing such workloads is still at an early stage, and, relevant to this work, relatively little is currently known about how LLM fine-tuning workloads run in practice. In this work, we address the knowledge gap by characterizing the execution of LLM fine-tuning workloads on clusters equipped with different GPUs, running LLM models at various scales. We analyze IBM's LLMFineTuningBench, a large-scale, diverse profiling dataset of 30,920 fine-tuning experiments that records both successful and failing configurations. We provide quantitative insight into throughput (expressed in tokens/s), scaling, failure, and potential for performance optimization for four commonly used GPU types, in setups of 1 to 32 GPUs. We find that (1) job feasibility (run or fail) depends on workload properties, with failure ratios rising from 52% for small batch sizes (16-64) up to 95% for the largest (1,024); (2) throughput grows logarithmically with batch size; (3) scaling is near-linear when the workload is deployed intra-node, and optimizations such as RoCE substantially improves efficiency for inter-node deployment (e.g., 0.72 vs. 0.26 efficiency without RoCE); and (4) system-level optimizations can outweigh application-level ones (RoCE, up to 2.9$\times$, vs. Fast MoE, 1.7$\times$).
item.dc:creator: Radu Nicolae, Daniele Lotito, Alexandru Iosup

item.title: Resource Locks and Fast Unlock for Shared Balances in Certificate-Based Payment Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.41207v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Certificate-based payment systems such as FastPay settle a payment with one round of signatures from a quorum of validators and avoid global ordering. The client collects the signatures, and validators never talk to each other. We observe that this client-driven design is complete only as long as no lock is ever undone. Each account has a single writer, a conflict can only come from that writer's own misbehavior, and the account stays locked as the penalty. Stablecoin payments routinely need balances that several accounts debit: treasuries, merchant pools, allowances and subscriptions. There, honest accounts race, locks must be undone, and a quorum certificate held privately by a client can be silently overridden. We prove that no unlock rule is safe in this setting unless certificate formation is visible to validators. We present a hybrid protocol. Personal accounts keep the client-driven FastPay path unchanged. A shared resource is a balance with its own version number and a set of authorized accounts. Transactions on shared resources are submitted to any validator and certified by a two-phase broadcast, ECHO then READY. The admission check requires both the sender's nonce and the resource's nonce to be free. Without contention, this path needs no consensus. When concurrent debits split the votes in any proportion, validators detect the split themselves, freeze the affected resource version, and resolve it with one agreement instance scoped to that version. Losing transactions return their sender nonce. We prove consistency, no overdraft, validity, finality and liveness. The protocol composes with the PDCC reconfiguration protocol.
item.dc:creator: Lingkang Shangguan

item.title: Falcons: Pushing the Speed-Ratio Limits of Lossy Compression for Parallel Scientific Applications
item.description: arXiv:2610.41209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The extreme volume of scientific data has become a critical challenge for modern exa-scale scientific computing applications, and error-bounded lossy compression remains indispensable for scientific data management due to its high data reduction rate and controllable data fidelity. However, to ensure sufficient data reduction, existing compressors incur prohibitive computational overheads in real-world parallel scientific computing applications. To overcome the performance bottlenecks of error-bounded lossy compression, we present \textbf{Falcons}, a broadly deployable error-bounded lossy compressor that simultaneously achieves \textbf{high compression ratios with ultra-fast throughput, minimizing the overhead in parallel scientific applications}. Falcons integrates three key designs: memory-regularized interpolation with SIMD (Single Instruction Multiple Data) vectorization, distribution-adaptive lossless coding, and application-oriented optimizations for multiple parallelization schemes. Across our evaluations on cutting-edge supercomputers, Falcons clearly outperforms state-of-the-art compressors, simultaneously achieving up to 29\% compression ratio improvement and 255\% throughput improvement. In case studies of real-world applications, Falcons accelerates large-scale parallel data I/O and remote transfer by up to 44.6\% and 51.5\%, and provides 1.55$\times$ end-to-end speedup for the full WRF (Weather Research \& Forecasting) application workflow.
item.dc:creator: Bing Lu, Jinyang Liu, Xinyang Ma, Quantong Fu, Chenwei Hou, Zedong Liu, Wenjing Huang, Yida Gu, Xingchen Liu, Zheng Wei, Anbang Wu, Xiaofeng Hou, Chao Li, Guangming Tan, Minyi Guo, Dingwen Tao

item.title: AuditFL: A Contract-Backed Clearing Layer for Open Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.41278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated learning (FL) keeps raw data local, but most deployments still rely on a trusted coordinator for client admission, checkpoint distribution, update collection, aggregation, and rewards. This paper presents AuditFL, a contract-backed clearing layer for auditable FL in open settings. AuditFL keeps training and aggregation off chain, stores model artifacts in an assumed reliable off-chain artifact store, and records only content identifiers and economic state on chain. Clients reserve update tickets with deposits, publish update identifiers, and later claim refunds or rewards; the task coordinator publishes global checkpoints and finalizes rounds through deterministic settlement rules. The design does not remove the aggregator, but makes its on-chain round decisions attributable, replayable, auditable, and economically constrained. We implement AuditFL as both a deterministic state-machine prototype and a Solidity contract on a local Ethereum-compatible Anvil chain. On full MNIST with Dirichlet non-IID splits, 12 rounds, and up to 200 clients, AuditFL preserves the Plain FL learning trajectory while its overhead follows closed-form control-plane models. At 200 clients, the contract run issues 5,026 transactions, stores 2,413 off-chain artifacts (144.9 MiB), and consumes 829.7M EVM gas, dominated by per-client reserve and publish calls. Controlled dropout, invalid-update, and artifact-unavailability stress tests reduce inclusion nearly linearly but still finalize rounds, with final-accuracy changes remaining within a few tenths of an accuracy percentage point even under high injected failure rates.
item.dc:creator: Alexandros Balla, Spyros Lalis

item.title: Migrating a Legacy Scientific Application with an AI Coding Agent: NICAM from Fortran to Kokkos
item.description: arXiv:2610.41313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Migrating from Fortran to C++/Kokkos broadens access to hardware accelerators through backends such as CUDA and HIP while offering greater flexibility in software design. However, legacy Fortran applications often have large codebases, making manual porting time-consuming and costly. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and AI coding agents have made large-scale code migration increasingly feasible. In this study, we ported NICAM (Nonhydrostatic ICosahedral Atmospheric Model), a legacy Fortran climate model accelerated with OpenACC, to C++/Kokkos with the assistance of Claude Code. The agent translated the code directly from Fortran to C++/Kokkos under human review. Approximately 140,000 lines of Fortran were analyzed and ported into 35,000 lines of C++/Kokkos, covering the dynamical core and seven physics packages. A 100-member ensemble comparison with the original Fortran model showed that the port is statistically consistent with the original. Performance was evaluated on Miyabi-G, an NVIDIA GH200 cluster, and Sirius, an AMD MI300A cluster. Compared with the Fortran/OpenACC baseline on GH200, the port achieved application speedups of $1.71\times$ on GH200 and $1.54\times$ on MI300A. The CUDA build achieved a GPU kernel-time speedup of $1.38\times$ on GH200. After normalization by peak memory bandwidth, the HIP build on MI300A achieved $0.96\times$ the kernel performance of the Fortran/OpenACC baseline.
item.dc:creator: Xuanzhengbo Ren, Takashi Shimokawabe, Hisashi Yashiro

item.title: RecIS: Unifying Sparse and Dense Computation for Efficient Recommendation Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.41457v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern recommender models scale sparse representations and dense computation together. They process thousands of heterogeneous feature fields, long user-behavior sequences, and trillion-scale Embedding parameters, while their dense networks increasingly use large Transformer architectures. The resulting execution mismatch creates fine-grained operations within stages, load imbalance and synchronization delays across devices, and GPU resource bubbles between stages. As models grow, these costs become a primary limit to scalable recommender training. Although existing systems improve Embedding caching and data prefetching, these inefficiencies still coexist in the GPU-centric workloads we study and jointly limit end-to-end throughput. We present RecIS, a unified framework for GPU-centric recommender training. RecIS treats the complete path from input features to dense computation as one optimization target and coordinates three complementary mechanisms. First, adaptive fusion combines fragmented feature transformations with vectorized memory access. Second, a GPU Embedding engine uses hash-based sharding and hierarchical communication to balance request placement and eliminate redundant transfers; it also specializes aggregation for forward and backward index structures. Third, a multistage pipeline overlaps input preparation for future iterations with dense computation in the current iteration. Together, these mechanisms reorganize a fragmented sparse front end into a dataflow that continuously feeds dense computation. We evaluate RecIS on representative industrial recommender models across distributed training platforms. Compared with PICASSO and TorchRec, RecIS reaches up to $2.62\times$ and $1.15\times$ their throughput, respectively, while reducing step latency by up to 61.5\% and 12.9\%. RecIS provides an efficient and scalable training system for large recommender models.
item.dc:creator: Hua Zong, Shuai Yang, Zhengxiong Zhou, Qingtao Zeng, Jiawei Liu, Hao Wan, Hongbin Zhou, Jiahao Wang, Hao Zhang, Bencheng Yan, Yuheng Huang, Huimin Yi, Jiamang Wang, Han Zhu, Jian Xu, Bo Zheng, Lin Qu

item.title: HiState: Hierarchical Prefix Cache Management for Hybrid LLM Serving in Agentic Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2610.41508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid large language models combine full-attention and recurrent linear layers to reduce inference costs. Prefix caching can further reduce redundant computation across requests, but a recurrent checkpoint cannot recover an earlier state corresponding to a shorter prefix. Existing hybrid prefix caching systems retain checkpoints at selected boundaries to support common reuse patterns in conventional conversations. However, agent workloads modify and revisit earlier contexts, exposing reusable prefixes whose checkpoints were never saved or have already been evicted. A straightforward approach is to retain more checkpoints to reduce recomputation, but their cumulative footprint can displace reusable prefixes from other sessions and cause additional cache misses. To address these problems, we present HiState, a prefix cache management system for hybrid models serving agent workloads. Our key observation is that prefix reuse accesses all matching key-value (KV) entries but only one recurrent checkpoint, regardless of how many checkpoints are retained. This asymmetry allows HiState to retain historical checkpoints on SSD while prioritizing fast memory for KV entries: each hit retrieves only one checkpoint whose size is independent of context length. Within this hierarchy, we propose adaptive interval control to balance checkpoint storage against recomputation, and unified eviction to coordinate checkpoint sparsification with reclamation of stale trajectories. We implement HiState on top of vLLM and evaluate it on two public coding-agent trace datasets and controlled microbenchmarks. On real agent traces, HiState achieves up to 5.73x and 5.44x speedups in p99 TTFT over vLLM-Marconi and SGLang-HiCache, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Zaifeng Pan, Lucas Wang, Xinwei Qiang, Yanbo Zhou, Chang Chen, Zhengding Hu, Yue Guan, Yufei Ding

item.title: MemX: Memory-Aware Automatic Parallelism for Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous GPU Training
item.description: arXiv:2610.41525v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cross-vendor heterogeneous GPU clusters are increasingly used for large-scale model training. However, their GPUs differ substantially in compute power, memory capacity, and interconnect characteristics. Existing automatic parallelism training systems usually minimize iteration time while treating memory as a hard constraint, almost failing in resolving the compute--memory asymmetry of cross-vendor clusters regardless correlation between memory and throughput. In this paper, we present MemX, a new memory-aware automatic parallelism system that jointly optimizes iteration time, peak memory usage, and cross-GPU memory balance. MemX consists of a weighted-product objective function, heterogeneous recomputation strategies, a minimal-set profiler, interpolation-based data augmentation, a dual-output XGBoost predictor, and a hash-signature prediction cache, in order to accelerate search of large-scale auto-parallel best configurations at lower cost. We implement MemX on Megatron-LM and evaluate it against four automatic parallelism baselines on two heterogeneous clusters. MemX achieves the lowest prediction Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 12.17% and is the only method that identifies the real Top-1 configuration under both time-based and memory-balance rankings. In terms of search cost and search space, MemX searches 31,240 configurations in 26.5 seconds, while an end-to-end profiling baseline is extrapolated to require about 17 days at the same scale. The simulation study that extends the measured 20-GPU data to 40-GPU and 60-GPU clusters further illustrates the effectiveness of MemX at larger scales.
item.dc:creator: Lin Meng, Yuzhong Sun, Jie Zhu

item.title: Where KV-Cache Error Lives in Looped Language Models: A Diagnostic Study of Ouro and Huginn
item.description: arXiv:2610.41825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A looped language model applies one block of layers 4 times per token and keeps a key/value (KV) plane for each loop. We study where storage error changes the next-token distribution and how shared-weight error accumulates, using Ouro-1.4B (4 loops) on GSM8K and MATH and Huginn-0125 (32 loops) on GSM8K-derived chains, with dense, simulated quantization. Per unit of error, values carry 94% of the diagonal Fisher mass, but measured KL is dominated by keys with larger quantization errors. Local second-order prediction follows the measured KL of typical sequences, including 136 held-out chains, but misses a few confident rows, and a local second-order factor for shared weights at 32 loops ranges from 1.65 (INT8) to 4.09 (INT4), so it depends on the error direction. A cell-level allocator lowers one-step KL at 25-48% of BF16 bytes, while paired task-accuracy comparisons depend on budget and the 25% gap against K4V2 shrinks to near zero under a post hoc answer-extraction check. A later Ouro-2.6B test retains the key/value split but falsifies measured-cost allocation's advantage over Fisher at 31%; across all 21 ledger registrations, 60 of 176 criteria failed.
item.dc:creator: Dezhen Lu, Runguo Li, Zixiang Ni, Yuchen Tang, Xingquan Kong, Jiaxing Yang, Jiarui Guo, Lingxiang Gao

item.title: A Deterministic Commitment Rule over Unstructured DAGs for Optimistic Replication
item.description: arXiv:2610.41837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In optimistic replication protocols, each replica uses the local state to execute requests from its clients in a wait-free manner, without synchronizing with other replicas. The outcomes may be revised later, making optimistic protocols only eventually consistent. To compensate for this consistency loss, an additional commitment mechanism can be employed: an underlying atomic broadcast protocol that allows replicas to periodically agree on the evolution of the object state. In this paper, we introduce a simple framework for optimistic replication based on a causality DAG: every replica represents the object state via a causally ordered set of client operations. The framework incorporates a deterministic commitment rule that incurs virtually zero message overhead beyond the basic dissemination of submitted operations.
item.dc:creator: Jo\~ao Paulo Bezerra, Petr Kuznetsov, L\'eo Olivier, Sara Tucci-Piergiovanni

item.title: Layered Reproducibility for High-Performance Computing Applications: The Feel++ and Ktirio Urban Buildings Case Study
item.description: arXiv:2610.41861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The High-Performance Computing (HPC) community struggles with reproducibility due to complex software stacks, heterogeneous hardware, and expensive validation cycles. This contribution presents a layered reproducibility strategy in which Feel++ provides a traceable software supply chain and Ktirio Urban Buildings (KUB) builds on it to manage versioned urban-building data, executable simulations, and checksum-verifiable result artifacts. Feel++ treats continuous integration (CI) plans, CMake presets, packaging manifests, public software metadata, operations commands, containers, software bill of materials (SBOM)/provenance metadata, and Feel++ Benchmarking reports for Feel++ and KUB cases as repositoryowned artifacts. KUB applies this foundation to City Energy Model Database (CEMDB) datasets, manifests, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) packaging, and verifiable outputs for computationally expensive simulations. The case study shifts reproducibility from late manual packaging to an artifact chain linking source commits, packages, containers, benchmark configurations, dataset versions, provenance records, and generated results.
item.dc:creator: Javier Cladellas (IRMA), Vincent Chabannes (IRMA), Christophe Prud'Homme (IRMA)

item.title: Decentralized Dynamic Stable Matching
item.description: arXiv:2610.41912v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study decentralized computation of the player-optimal stable matching (POSM) with unannounced player arrivals and departures. Without a common clock, event information, or direct communication, players propose to arms and observe only their own accept/reject outcomes. Mismatch cost counts rounds when the realized matching differs from the current POSM. For known preferences, we give a deterministic polynomial-time self-calibrating protocol with cost $O(t_*+K^2\log T)$, improving the previous bound $O(T^{1-1/K}(\log T)^{2/K})$. Here $K$ is the number of arms, $t_*$ the last event time, and $T$ the horizon. Players use only local time and proposal outcomes, knowing neither $t_*$ nor $T$. For any nondecreasing, polynomial-time-computable $g(t)=\Omega(t)$, the protocol achieves $O(g(t_*)+K^2N_g(T))$. Here $g$ governs recovery time, while $N_g(T)$ counts iterations of $t\mapsto t+g(t)$ below $T$, exposing a tradeoff between recovery time and asymptotic mismatch cost. Any randomized protocol with recovery scale $g(t)\ge1$ and sublinear asymptotic mismatch cost has worst-case expected cost $\Omega(t_*+N_g(T))$. Thus, with $g(t)=t$, our protocol is optimal up to a $K^2$ factor among sublinear-cost protocols with $O(t_*)$ recovery time. For unknown preferences on both sides, each player and arm learns its preferences from its own observations after matching. We give a decentralized learning protocol with expected cost $O(t_*+K^4\Delta_{\mathrm{min}}^{-2}\log T)$, where $\Delta_{\mathrm{min}}$ measures preference gaps. A complementary static-setting lower bound adapted from the literature shows that the dependence on $T$ and $\Delta_{\mathrm{min}}$ is tight.
item.dc:creator: Jing Chen, Mengtong Gao, Zhenhe Zhang

item.title: Matching Workloads to Blackwell: Power-Resolved Benchmarking of NVIDIA B200 and B300 across HPC and AI Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2610.41919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We evaluate NVIDIA B200 and B300 (Blackwell Ultra) GPUs on two independent eight-GPU clusters, spanning computer-vision inference and training, LLM inference with Llama-3-8B and 70B~\cite{llama3}, and six production HPC codes. The B300 is not a uniform successor to the B200: it trails by up to 5.6$\times$ on convolutional inference, 8$\times$ on 3D vision transformer training, 24--27\% on 70B LLM throughput, and 16$\times$ on double-precision Quantum ESPRESSO. We resolve the convolutional deficit using per-GPU board power rather than throughput alone: on the affected workloads the B300 draws only 36--53\% of its 1100\,W envelope, whereas on ViT-Large, which it wins, both parts saturate at 95--97\% of TDP. Because our harness keeps inputs resident in device memory, a host-side data pipeline is excluded by construction, localizing the cause to per-kernel cost. Two B300 nodes of identical silicon differ by 2.1$\times$ in time-to-first-token solely from a development vLLM build. We give per-workload procurement guidance.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Zand, Trung Dac Nguyen, H. Birali Runesha

item.title: An Incentive-Aligned Trust-Centric Coordination Layer for Heterogeneous Blockchain Interoperability
item.description: arXiv:2610.41032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The interoperability between permissioned and public blockchains is hampered by asymmetric privacy, trust, and governance assumptions. We propose a coordination architecture that decouples cross-domain trust management and privacy enforcement from underlying blockchain protocols, requiring no protocol-level modifications. The framework integrates cryptographic unlinkability mechanisms with incentive-compatible relay selection, combining stake-weighted participation and temporally accumulated reputation to align economic commitment with sustained correctness. We formalize the adversarial model and derive security and privacy properties for cross-domain coordination, demonstrating robustness against Sybil infiltration, collusion, and strategic stake concentration. Simulation-based analysis characterizes key design trade-offs between quorum thresholds, reputation memory, and anonymity parameters, indicating that privacy-preserving coordination can be achieved without degrading responsiveness or incentive stability when parameters are properly tuned.
item.dc:creator: Saeed Moradi, Sara Rouhani

item.title: ZenKO: Guided and Iterative Quantum-Classical Method for Molecular Electronic Structure using Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
item.description: arXiv:2610.41146v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The electronic structure of molecules is foundational for scientific advancement, however determining it remains challenging due to the growth of the molecular Hilbert space with system size. Recent approaches address this by using quantum circuits to sample candidate configurations and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) to compute the ground state. We propose ZenKO, a novel gradient-based, iterative SQD method that employs a hybrid quantum-classical approach. ZenKO decomposes configuration selection into discovery, validation, and refinement, enabling targeted subspace expansion and guided exploration. Our evaluation demonstrates that, across $H_2O$, $H_{10}$, and $N_2$ molecules, ZenKO improves ground-state accuracy compared to prior iterative methods, while significantly reducing classical cost.
item.dc:creator: Aditya Ranjan, Devesh Tiwari

item.title: ARK: Avoiding Routing Collisions for KV Cache Transfer in Disaggregated LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.41160v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Disaggregated LLM inference separates the prefill and decode phases across GPU pools, generating massive KV-cache transfers. Because these transfers last hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, they behave as mega elephant flows that dominate link bandwidth utilization. In this regime, stateless ECMP can perform poorly: hash collisions may overload one spine link while leaving others idle, stretching transfer times by seconds. Yet this same persistence makes coordination practical. Since these flows are long-lived, even lightweight one-to-all coordination can be amortized over their lifetime. We present ARK, a distributed elephant-flow path reservation mechanism. ARK coordinates senders to choose source ports whose hashes map concurrent flows onto distinct spines, without requiring switch changes or receiver-side packet reordering. Packet-level RDMA simulations show that ARK reduces mean and P95 FCT by up to 27.3% and 34.0% under moderate load, and further reduces mean TTFT by up to 12.9%.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: In Proceedings of the ACM SIGCOMM 2026 Conference (SIGCOMM '26), pp. 2067-2073, 2026
item.dc:creator: Hung-Chun Lin, Ting-Wei Hsu, Chung-En Ho, Ahmed Saeed

item.title: TIRx: A Unified Tile Primitive ML Compiler Across Heterogeneous Backends
item.description: arXiv:2601.19092v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern ML kernels evolve rapidly with new optimizations and hardware features. ML compiler abstractions must accommodate richer memory hierarchies, more forms of thread cooperation, and increasingly heterogeneous backends while retaining the control required for peak performance. We present TIRx, an ML compiler for GPUs and AI accelerators that exposes these ingredients through explicit interfaces. TIRx introduces an explicit execution-scope abstraction that captures participating hardware teams at multiple granularities. It also uses tensor layouts to map logical tensors to heterogeneous hardware spaces through named axes and shard/replica/offset semantics. Finally, it introduces tile-primitive dispatch, which lowers high-level operations to efficient implementations according to scope, layout, and backend. This design preserves native-level control while automating recurring address calculation, operand preparation, and instruction-loop generation. Our evaluation shows vendor-level performance across the latest GPUs and AI accelerators, while native-code case studies show substantial reductions in low-level implementation code.
item.dc:creator: Bohan Hou, Hongyi Jin, Guanjie Wang, Shushi Hong, Jinqi Chen, Yaxing Cai, Lijie Yang, Zihao Ye, Yaoyao Ding, Ruihang Lai, Todd Mowry, Tianqi Chen

item.title: Porting and Benchmarking Chapel on Emerging RISC-V Hardware: An HPC Viability Study
item.description: arXiv:2608.14799v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Chapel programming language recently added support for the RISC-V architecture. Here we discuss what changes were needed for Chapel to work on RISC-V as well as lessons learned from the porting process. We use some of Chapel's extensive benchmark suite to gain further insight into the suitability of the RISC-V architecture for future HPC use. We compare performance on SiFive P550 and Unmatched boards and a Sophon SG2042 with a variety of other recent HPC CPU platforms. Various portability and performance anomalies arose on different architectures and are discussed. While the RISC-V machines represent smaller preliminary offerings and not HPC-class hardware, these results still provide hope that RISC-V hardware can become viable for HPC in the near future.
item.dc:creator: Ian Henriksen, Chris Taylor, Patrick Diehl, Jade Abraham, Palmer Cox, Bradford L. Chamberlain, Stephen L. Olivier

item.title: Communication-Aware Qubit Placement and Automatic Node-Count Allocation for Distributed State-Vector Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2610.09659v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum circuit simulation enables the execution of large-scale quantum algorithms by partitioning qubits across multiple computational nodes. However, an inefficient qubit placement leads to excessive inter-node communication, limiting performance and scalability. This work introduces a framework that computes a communication-aware qubit placement offline, minimizing data exchange among nodes, and selects, before circuit execution, the largest node count whose performance degradation stays below a user-defined threshold. The framework is integrated with the QuEST simulator. Evaluations on synthetic benchmarks and real-world QASMBench circuits show that optimized placements reduce communication and achieve runtime speedups of up to 2.3x over the identity placement, particularly in circuits with sparse, structured interactions. Our results show that qubit placement strongly affects the efficiency of distributed simulation and provide a practical, resource-scalable solution for quantum workload
item.dc:creator: \'I\~nigo Ar\'ejula-A\'isa, Sergio Iserte, Petter Sand{\aa}s, Ricard S. Raigada-Garc\'ia, Antonio J. Pe\~na

item.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2610.22731v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.
item.dc:creator: RuiLong Jiang, Dustin Rhodes, Danny McCormick, Yuta Labur, Reza Rokni

item.title: Recency Is the Wrong Axis: A Negative Result on Windowed Deepest-Plane KV Caching in Looped Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.34436v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Looped language models reuse one block of layers over $R$ recurrent steps but store a key-value (KV) plane for each step. Keeping only the deepest plane shrinks the cache up to $R$-fold. A natural repair, which we call RIPE, keeps every plane for the $W$ most recent positions and shares the deepest plane elsewhere. This repair acts on the wrong axis: across three looped models, the cost of sharing is set by how far the late loops' planes have converged (ripeness) and by which positions share, not by recency. On Raven-Llama the deep planes sit within the bf16 rounding floor, so no window is needed. On Huginn-0125 a 64-position window removes most of a concentrated replay-error tail (9 to 1 positions over 48 prompts), yet in a real self-speculative decoder the policy is slower and larger than the deepest plane alone and not measurably closer to full-cache decoding. On Ouro-1.4B the prompt lies outside any 16-64-position window: on 24 GSM8K questions with a 2048-token budget, the full cache and a FlashLoop baseline finish 23 answers and RIPE at most 2, although physical storage matches the emulated policy bitwise. Sensitivity and ripening models fitted on Huginn and Raven explain their contrast, and Ouro's own report that prompt-side sharing is harmful explains the third. Separately, bf16 execution-shape effects are as large as the cache effects being measured. Recent-window repair of shared-plane caches should not be adopted without a per-model ripeness test. We release ten pre-registered batches with every failed prediction.
item.dc:creator: Dezhen Lu, Runguo Li, Zixiang Ni, Yuchen Tang, Xingquan Kong, Jiaxing Yang, Jiarui Guo

item.title: AMMA: A Multi-Chiplet Memory-Centric Architecture for Low-Latency 1M Context Attention Serving
item.description: arXiv:2604.26103v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: All current LLM serving systems place the GPU at the center, from production-level attention-FFN disaggregation to NVIDIA's Rubin GPU-LPU heterogeneous platform. Even academic PIM/PNM proposals still treat the GPU as the central hub for cross-device communication. Yet the GPU's compute-rich architecture is fundamentally mismatched with the memory-bound nature of decode-phase attention, inflating serving latency while wasting power and die area on idle compute units. The problem is compounded as reasoning and agentic workloads push context lengths toward one million tokens, making attention latency the primary user-facing bottleneck. To address these inefficiencies, we present AMMA, a multi-chiplet, memory-centric architecture for low-latency long-context attention. AMMA replaces GPU compute dies with HBM-PNM cubes, roughly doubling the available memory bandwidth to better serve memory-bound attention workloads. To translate this bandwidth into proportional performance gains, we introduce (i) a logic-die microarchitecture that fully exploits per-cube internal bandwidth for decode attention under a minimal power and area budget, (ii) a two-level hybrid parallelism scheme, and (iii) a reordered collective flow that reduces intra-chip die-to-die communication overhead. We further conduct a design-space exploration over per-cube compute power and intra-chip D2D link bandwidth, providing actionable guidance for hardware designers. Evaluations show that AMMA achieves 15.5X lower attention latency and 6.9X lower energy consumption compared with the NVIDIA H100.
item.dc:creator: Zhongkai Yu, Haotian Ye, Chenyang Zhou, Ohm Rishabh Venkatachalam, Zaifeng Pan, Zhengding Hu, Junsung Kim, Won Woo Ro, Po-An Tsai, Shuyi Pei, Yangwook Kang, Yufei Ding

item.title: TileMaxSim: Roofline Regimes and Compression Limits for Fused GPU MaxSim Scoring
item.description: arXiv:2606.26439v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: MaxSim scoring dominates the cost of multi-vector retrieval. Several groups built fused GPU kernels for it independently during 2026, and all report one measure of success: the fraction of peak memory bandwidth reached. That measure assumes the operator is limited by the bytes it moves. We show the assumption fails in two ways, and that two other quantities decide performance: which side of the roofline ridge a shape falls on, and how many dependent gathers the scoring path performs. We first locate the boundary. Fused arithmetic intensity is Nq*Nd /(Nq + Nd) FLOP per byte, against an H100 dense-FP16 ridge of 295.4. The operator is therefore memory-bound at ColBERT shapes and compute-bound at ColPali-scale query lengths. Published analyses report one side each and do not reconcile them. We measure the crossover at three document lengths, and a closed form predicts it inside the measured bracket each time. Past the crossover, percent of peak bandwidth falls to 4% while percent of peak FLOPs rises above 40%. The reported measure is therefore defined on only one side of a boundary that real workloads cross. We also validate the underlying traffic model against DRAM counters, to 0.003%. We then show that moving fewer bytes does not make the kernel faster. Fusing product-quantized asymmetric distance computation into the kernel moves 15.9x fewer bytes than exact FP16 on tensor cores and runs 3.0x slower. Counters rule out the usual causes: it reaches 1.23% of peak DRAM throughput at 98.2% occupancy. The limit is 6.5*10^9 dependent gathers, a count that does not fall when the codes get smaller. A hand-written CUDA version with a staged table recovers 4.7x and remains slower than exact scoring. Finally, we give the first head-to-head comparison of three fused MaxSim kernels, over 28 shapes, with every result checked against an exhaustive FP32 reference.
item.dc:creator: Ashutosh Sharma

item.title: GPUSparse: Fast and Exact Learned Sparse Retrieval on a GPU-Resident Inverted Index
item.description: arXiv:2606.26441v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Learned sparse models such as SPLADE match the quality of dense bi-encoders and keep the exact-match behavior of lexical retrieval. They are served on CPUs, using inverted-index traversal algorithms such as WAND. These algorithms are fast because they prune: they skip documents that cannot enter the top-k. Pruning makes the result approximate, and its control flow is sequential and datadependent, which suits a CPU and not a GPU. We argue that a GPU should not run a faster traversal. It should remove traversal altogether. A GPU has enough memory bandwidth to score every posting, so exactness need not be traded for speed. We present GPUSparse, which keeps the inverted index in GPU memory and scores queries with one fused scatter-add kernel. Nothing is pruned. GPUSparse searches all 8.8M MS MARCO passages in 1.27 ms per query, at 787 queries per second on one H100. Its results are exact: Recall@10, @100 and @1000 against an exhaustive FP32 reference are all 1.000, and quality at full scale matches Pyserini's exact SPLADE retrieval to three decimals. Exactness costs hardware rather than latency. Under core pinning, one H100 is worth about seven CPU cores. GPUSparse is 5.6x faster than one core and 2.8x slower than a 32-core socket. A CPU socket is therefore cheaper for approximate serving. The GPU is the better choice when exactness is required, where GPUSparse is 3.0x faster than exact CPU block-max pruning. We also decompose GPU latency. Traversal takes 55 to 80% of it and selection 18 to 38%, and the split moves with scale, which reconciles three conflicting published reports.
item.dc:creator: Ashutosh Sharma

item.title: How Much Reconstruction Does Quantum Machine Learning Need? Late Fusion of Uncoupled Quantum Subcircuits
item.description: arXiv:2608.05595v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Circuit cutting lets a large quantum neural network (QNN) run as independent subcircuits on small devices, but rebuilding its outputs by quasiprobability reconstruction carries a classical sampling overhead exponential in the number of cuts. This paper asks whether machine-learning tasks need this step. We replace it with late fusion: subcircuits are trained without cross-cut coupling, and a small classical head combines their local measurements at a cost constant in the cut count. To characterize the trade-off, we introduce a reconstruction dial $Q$, a physically executable budget that retains a fraction of the quasiprobability terms, and a cut-entanglement diagnostic that indicates, within a fixed scale, how much reconstruction a task needs (Spearman $\rho=0.59$ over $104$ runs). Across synthetic and standard datasets, uncoupled late fusion is equivalent to full reconstruction within a predefined margin of $0.02$ accuracy on most benchmarks and pooled over the controlled sweep, at exponentially lower cost; deficits of $0.02$-$0.04$ remain on the most cross-cut tasks. Fusion tops the dial's accuracy/cost frontier, is more robust to shot and device noise, and loses nothing as the coupled model's entangling depth grows. We state the exact condition under which fusion must lose accuracy, a decision-relevant cross-cut correlator, and realize it with entangled-state inputs; for classical inputs the register partition discards no information. We claim no advantage over classical machine learning.
item.dc:creator: Prabhjot Singh, Adel N. Toosi, Rajkumar Buyya

item.title: On the Expressiveness of Asynchronous Processes with Nested Session Types (Extended Version)
item.description: arXiv:2610.32558v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Session types are a type-based approach to correct message-passing programs, where types specify protocols for channels and type checking guarantees communication correctness. Traditional session types express regular protocols only, which leaves out many protocols found in practice. Aiming at overcoming this limitation, Nested Session Types (NSTs) can specify nested recursive protocols. NSTs are known to be characterised by one-counter machines and deterministic context-free languages. In this paper, we study the expressiveness of ASP (Asynchronous Session Processes), the process model associated with NSTs as introduced by Das et al. We prove that AST is Turing complete by giving a correct encoding of two-counter machines into typed processes. Our encoding uses a non-trivial state-aware representation of counters and instructions that is neatly governed by NSTs.
item.dc:creator: Sjors Wortelboer, Dan Frumin, Jorge A. P\'erez

item.title: From GPU to TPU with Coding Agents: What Works, What Fails, and What It Costs?
item.description: arXiv:2610.34422v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A coding agent can migrate a machine learning workload, report success, and still change how the model trains. Rising compute costs, limited accelerator capacity, and vendor dependence are pushing organizations toward alternatives to graphics processing units (GPUs); a key question is whether agent-generated migrations to tensor processing units (TPUs) can be trusted and at what cost. We build a dataset of 148 PyTorch ML research projects and use Claude Code to migrate ten of them from NVIDIA GPUs to Google Cloud TPUs. We independently assess whether each migration runs, preserves numerical behavior, executes on the intended hardware, maintains the project's goal, and delivers acceptable performance. We also examine failures, human effort, and costs. Eight projects meet our project-goal criterion, and migrations require 2.4 human interventions on average. Of 70 execution attempts, 53 fail (76%), and 26 of these failures (49%) raise no error. The most frequent cause is repeated compilation and other execution inefficiencies, while interactions with third-party libraries can silently change the computation: in one four-chip migration, the agent reports success despite a change in gradient clipping that reduces accuracy from 86.53% to 84.89%. Execution costs vary widely: in one workload, TorchTPU, a PyTorch execution backend for TPUs, trains 1.86 times faster and 25% cheaper per run than the GPU. For practitioners, these findings motivate independent reference runs, verification under the intended hardware configuration, and workload-specific acceptance and stopping criteria that account for both computational and human costs.
item.dc:creator: Hui Sun, Anderson Uch\^oa, Wesley K. G. Assun\c{c}\~ao

item.title: SeQUeNCe.DQC: Full-stack Simulation of Distributed Quantum Computing
item.description: arXiv:2610.39476v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Distributed quantum computing (DQC) connects multiple quantum processing units to overcome the scale limits of monolithic hardware. We introduce SeQUeNCe$.$DQC a new top-level module within the SeQUeNCe package that compiles monolithic circuits into topology-aware execution plans and coordinates their execution using SeQUeNCe's existing quantum-network modules and protocols. We validate SeQUeNCe$.$DQC by reproducing a two-node trapped-ion Grover experiment in simulation and comparing success probabilities with the reported 71% benchmark. We then evaluate how compiler strategy, topology, and memory capacity jointly govern distributed circuit execution time and success rate. In these experiments, our hybrid compilers successfully identified mixed TeleGate/TeleData execution plans that outperformed pure gate-teleportation strategies. By capturing the physical overhead of distributed quantum primitives, SeQUeNCe$.$DQC provides a rigorous platform for co-designing DQC software and hardware architectures.
item.dc:creator: Sanjay Suresh, Caitao Zhan, Joaquin Chung, Rajkumar Kettimuthu
